description: Core Spanish verbs and patterns for A2–B1 learners (ser/estar, hay, have, want, can, must, go, come, like), Latin American Spanish.

terms.definition: Says what or who something is: name, job, origin, or a lasting trait.
terms.example: Soy Ana, soy de Colombia y soy enfermera. — I'm Ana, from Colombia, a nurse.
terms.mental_model: ser is the name tag you wear every day; estar is today's status update.

terms.definition: There is or there are: points out that something exists somewhere.
terms.example: ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí? — Is there a pharmacy around here?
terms.discussion: Hay stays the same for one or many: hay un banco, hay dos bancos. Follow it with un, una or a number, not el or la.

terms.definition: Want: asks for a thing, or says what you'd like to do.
terms.example: Quiero un café con leche, por favor. — I'd like a latte, please.
terms.discussion: At a counter, 'Quiero un…, por favor' sounds normal, not rude. 'Me da un…, por favor' is just as common.

terms.definition: Must or have to: says something is necessary for you to do.
terms.example: Tengo que trabajar mañana temprano. — I have to work early tomorrow.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Tengo ir' or 'Tengo a ir': the que is required. Say 'Tengo que ir'.

terms.definition: Tells where someone or something is, or how they feel right now.
terms.example: Estoy en el bus y estoy cansada. — I'm on the bus, and tired.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Mi casa es en el centro' for where your house is: say 'Mi casa está en el centro'.

terms.definition: Go: move to another place, away from where you are now.
terms.example: Los sábados voy al mercado. — On Saturdays I go to the market.
terms.discussion: a + el becomes al: voy al cine, voy a la playa. And '¡Vamos!' on its own means 'Let's go!'

terms.definition: Like, turned around: the thing you like is the subject, and you come first as me or te.
terms.example: Me gustan los tacos de mi abuela. — I like my grandma's tacos.
terms.mental_model: Read it as 'please': me gusta el café is 'coffee pleases me', so the verb follows the coffee.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Yo gusto los tacos': that says you please the tacos. Say 'Me gustan los tacos'.

terms.definition: Have: owning things, plus your age and body states like hunger or cold.
terms.example: Mi hijo tiene seis años. — My son is six.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Soy seis años' or 'Estoy hambre': say 'Tengo seis años' and 'Tengo hambre'.

terms.definition: Can: says you're able or allowed to do something, and makes polite requests.
terms.example: ¿Puedes mandarme el archivo hoy? — Can you send me the file today?

terms.definition: Come: move toward the place where the speaker is, or will be.
terms.example: ¿Vienes a mi fiesta el sábado? — Coming to my party Saturday?
terms.anti_example: Not 'Ya vengo' when a friend calls you to the door: say 'Ya voy'. 'Ya vengo' means 'I'll be right back'.

relationships.description: Both translate English be: ser for what something is, estar for where it is or how it is now.
Add que and an infinitive to tener and have becomes have to.
ir moves away from the speaker, venir moves toward the speaker.
